## Example 1.3 {#iv1-example-1-3 .vector-lesson}

The wireframe shows a cube divided into eight smaller cubes. Each small edge represents 1 unit in space.

::: {.v-example-layout}
<div>
<p><strong>a)</strong> Draw one more copy of <span data-math="\underset{\sim}{a}"></span>.</p>
<p><strong>b)</strong> Draw <span data-math="-\underset{\sim}{a}"></span>.</p>
<p><strong>c)</strong> Draw a unit vector and label it <span data-math="\underset{\sim}{u}"></span>.</p>
</div>
<div>
<img class="v-cube-figure" src="../media/example-1-3.svg" alt="Original booklet wireframe: a cube divided into eight smaller cubes, with vector a and its dotted vertical projection.">
</div>
:::

<div class="booklet-cue">Booklet Example 1.3 · p. 4</div>

::: notes
Preserve the supplied spatial diagram. Vector a rises two small vertical edges and goes one small edge in each of the two horizontal spatial directions. One possible translated copy starts at the front-face bottom midpoint and ends at the top-face right-edge midpoint. A copy may extend outside the displayed cube; equality requires the same spatial magnitude and direction. Reverse the drawn arrow for −a. Any small cube edge supplies a unit vector. Apparent lengths in a perspective drawing do not measure actual spatial lengths; do not accept arbitrary equal screen lengths as proof of equality.
:::
